title: Trails Through the Night Sky
caption: Star trails around Polaris above Kitt Peak National Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The scene looks like daytime, but star trails circle through the night sky in this long exposure of NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). On the highest peak stands the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. Almost directly above it, at the center of the rings of star trails, sits Polaris, the North Star.

Polaris stays put because it lies at the north celestial pole, in line with the axis Earth spins around. As the planet turns, every other star seems to wheel around it, and a long exposure records those paths as arcs.

On the horizon, the lights of Tucson, Arizona, glow yellow about 89 kilometers (55 miles) to the northeast. NOIRLab's citizen science campaign Globe at Night invites stargazers of every age to help monitor light pollution in their own cities, wherever in the world they live.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph of Kitt Peak credited to KPNO/NOIRLab. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Light from nearby towns brightens the sky and makes faint objects harder to study, which is why a glow like Tucson's matters to observatories. Campaigns such as Globe at Night gather measurements of that glow from many places at once.
alt: Concentric star trails circling Polaris above the Mayall telescope on Kitt Peak, with the yellow glow of Tucson on the horizon.
